name: Elena Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What fills your workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the stair and door crew on a new block of flats. A trade certificate started me off, but twenty years of carpentry taught me when a drawing does not fit a slab. I like seeing a staircase go in cleanly for people who will live there.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Cold mornings in my knees and managers who rush the second check. My partner Adil works at a repair shop; we have two children in school, a mortgage and about four months saved. I am the site union rep, and I have never used AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the housing crew that a small office shortcut changes no one’s need for a level stair. I would ask the site union group to keep pressing for safe staffing after the AI fuss dies down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Adil earns at a repair shop, and we have around four months of expenses saved. The mortgage and two children’s school costs are steady, and my carpenter pay is ordinary; a plateau keeps our budget manageable but not loose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the stair and door team on the current flats. At the next union site meeting I would bring the two rushed staircase jobs to ask for a second skilled checker before sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about managers rushing us, but calm about next month’s income. The same problems remain even if AI does little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What went wrong on the rushed stairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stair can be tidy on paper and wrong under a worker’s foot. We stopped one bad rise before fixing the treads, but I want a second checker every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to review the drawings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used an AI tool and do not need one to check a rise with a tape and a colleague.

say: I would tell the crew **stairs and doors** still need skilled site checks.
I would raise a **second-checker rule** at the union site meeting.
think: Our **four-month cushion** and two wages keep the mortgage manageable.
Rushed **staffing** worries me more than limited AI in the office.
do: Bring two **near misses** to the next union site meeting for a checker rule.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed work, with own job and household pay secure.
S0.quote: A stair can be tidy on paper and wrong under a worker’s foot.
fieldNote: She sees no realistic AI income loss in the plateau, but **existing safety pressure** remains.
The union action is a specific **second-checker demand** based on two near misses.

steps.text: Keep leading flat stairs and door fitting
Bring two stair near misses to union site meeting for second checker rule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can book materials faster, but I will not sign a stair from an untested drawing. I would ask our union branch to agree who checks a machine-produced schedule before it reaches the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning jobs may shrink first, but the contractor may use faster schedules to squeeze our carpentry hours between flats. Adil’s repair shop wage and our savings help, yet a run of shorter weeks would change the mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep written records of paid hours on the next three flat blocks. If those hours fall, I would delay the family’s planned holiday and ask the union group to bargain for a minimum paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a plausible hours cut. I dislike new software, but I am more concerned about a foreman’s wage disappearing between jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the union group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three block rosters, the actual clocked hours and the pay slips. A complaint without numbers is easy for management to put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Adil’s wages cover a shortfall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, but not all of the mortgage if my weeks stay short. We would preserve the four-month reserve as long as possible.

say: I would require a **human stair check** before AI schedules drive site targets.
I would ask the **union group** to bargain for a minimum paid week.
think: A faster plan could bring **shorter carpentry weeks** between flat blocks.
Adil’s wage and savings cushion the gap, but cannot replace my **full pay** indefinitely.
do: Record **three blocks** of paid site hours and slips.
Delay the **family holiday** if hours fall.
Bring the **minimum-week proposal** to the union group with rosters.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic reduction in paid hours.
S1.quote: A complaint without numbers is easy for management to put aside.
fieldNote: She uses measured **paid hours** rather than vague anger to support bargaining.
The holiday cut is conditional on a **real pay fall**, while mortgage payments take priority.

steps.text: Delay the family holiday only after paid carpentry hours fall
Bring three rosters to union group to seek a minimum paid week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site crew that thinking AI in 2028 can draft a staircase, but a robot cannot fit it until around 2031. I would demand a real occupied-building trial before a contractor cuts the joiners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose carpentry days once those robots arrive, and I will be only forty eight with a mortgage and two children. Four months saved and some local builders give us time, but I cannot let a likely pay cut become a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my site shifts and ask the union branch for a written trial and staffing plan. If two rosters show fewer paid days, I would apply to posted nearby carpentry jobs and leave only for a firm offer that covers the mortgage and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not sleepless. I have a plan and a small cushion, although I do not like how quickly this arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you travel farther for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a posted job with a firm wage that covers the extra trip and the mortgage. I would not resign for a hopeful conversation at a site gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the robot trial include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An uneven stairwell and a worker who can stop the machine. A neat empty room is not enough proof for a building people will live in.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** drafts stairs before capable fitting robots arrive around 2031.
I would demand an **occupied-building trial** and staffing notice through the union.
think: My **paid days** could shrink when robots reach hands-on carpentry.
A **four-month reserve** and some nearby builders give us time to search.
do: Keep **site shifts** while the contractor pays them.
Ask the **union branch** for trial and staffing plans.
Apply to **posted nearby carpentry roles** after two reduced rosters, leaving only for mortgage-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hours loss while retaining a practical fallback.
S2.quote: I would not resign for a hopeful conversation at a site gate.
fieldNote: Her concern is a realistic **carpentry pay cut**, not immediate displacement by thinking AI.
Applications require **posted vacancies** and firm mortgage-covering wages after two reduced rosters.

steps.text: Keep paid flat carpentry shifts while contractor hours continue
Ask union branch for robot trial and staffing plan
Apply to posted nearby carpenter roles after two reduced rosters for firm mortgage-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives the builders time to test a stair robot on old slabs and train people to stop it. I would still want the union’s safety rep on that test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 changes drawings first; the robot comes around 2034 when I am fifty one. I still need work then, and I could take a paid quality-check role if one is actually posted, but I will not buy a course on a maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the stairs crew this year and request the company’s paid quality-control training plan. If a funded course with paid hours and a posted checker vacancy paying enough for our mortgage appears, I would complete it and apply; otherwise I would stay in carpentry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about future hours, though the longer run gives us choices. I will learn a new check when the job is real and the hours are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol before the vacancy is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A course enquiry is easy; losing paid site days for an uncertain role is not. I need the posted wage and paid time in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would quality checking involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Measuring the stair rise after installation and checking the fasteners a robot used. I would want authority to reject unsafe work, not just sign a sheet.

say: I would seek **old-slab trials** and a union safety rep before 2034 stair robots spread.
I would ask for **paid quality training** tied to a posted checker role.
think: I still need **carpentry wages** around 2034 and later.
A **checker job** might help, but I would not count an unposted role.
do: Keep leading **stair fitting** while paid shifts continue.
Complete **funded quality training** only with paid hours and a posted mortgage-covering checker vacancy.
**Apply** for the posted checker vacancy after funded training only if its wage covers the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about later hours, with a conditional paid route to learn.
S3.quote: A course enquiry is easy; losing paid site days for an uncertain role is not.
fieldNote: She distinguishes asking about a course from actually taking **funded training**.
The role must be **posted, paid and mortgage-covering**, preserving household conditions in the action.

steps.text: Keep leading paid staircase fitting shifts
Complete funded checker course only with paid hours and posted mortgage-covering vacancy
Apply after funded checker course for posted role only at mortgage-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices ten years is time to learn a proper stair before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. I would keep pushing for safe staffing rather than waiting for a machine date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty six when capable robots arrive and still expect to need my wage. Our four-month reserve is a cushion, not a salary. Adil’s repair-shop pay may not cover the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the stair crew working during 2026 and pay an extra twenty from each wage into savings if the mortgage and children’s costs are covered first. In the first year after 2036 I would review actual paid hours and posted local jobs before choosing a course; if 2039 robots cut shifts, I would apply only for a firm mortgage-covering role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the long-run wage risk, but ten years gives me room to build a reserve. I would rather prepare with real pay than chase a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra twenty come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From each paid wage after the mortgage and school costs, not from moving the four-month reserve around. If Adil loses hours, we would pause the extra transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We still have a mortgage and two school-age children now, and I expect to need paid work in my fifties.

say: I would protect **apprentice practice** before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 carpentry robots.
I would keep bargaining for **safe staffing** through the union.
think: I expect to need **paid work** around 2039, even with a moderate cushion.
Adil’s pay alone may not cover the **mortgage** if my hours shrink.
do: Keep **2026 stair shifts** while paid work is available.
Save an extra **twenty from each wage** only after mortgage, school costs and Adil’s hours allow.
feel: **Anxious** about a distant income risk, with present work secure and time to add reserves.
S4.quote: Our four-month reserve is a cushion, not a salary.
fieldNote: This is actual **new saving from wages**, conditional on core bills and Adil’s hours.
She keeps later job applications tied to **posted firm pay**, not unconfirmed training or vacancies.

steps.text: Keep paid staircase fitting shifts during 2026
Save twenty from each wage only after core bills and Adil’s hours allow
Review actual paid hours and posted local jobs after 2036 before choosing training
Apply if 2039 robots cut shifts only for firm mortgage-covering work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could cut staircase work by 2031 while the mortgage remains. A written staffing plan, posted jobs with a proper wage and paid quality-check training would help us make decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs a staircase after a robot fits it. A family walks on the steps, not on the contractor’s promises.

headlineQuote: A family walks on the steps, not on the contractor’s promises.
portrait: **Elena**, 43, is a skilled stair-and-door lead with a trade certificate, typical pay and about four months saved.
She and Adil support **two school-age children** and a mortgage, with some nearby building jobs available.
She avoids **AI tools**, represents the crew at union meetings and would train only for a funded posted role.
The **2028 case** worries her because 2031 robots may shrink paid carpentry days while she still needs wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce staircase shifts around 2031 while the family needs her wage.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan**, posted mortgage-covering jobs and paid checker training would help.
